# Architecture & Backend Scaffold {#sec-architecture}

This chapter is the technical foundation for everything that follows. It
explains how PhyloTrace is assembled as a program: how it starts, how it is
divided into modules, how those modules find and talk to one another, and where
the boundary lies between the R application and the external bioinformatics
tools it drives. Later chapters describe individual components; this chapter
describes the scaffold they are built on.

## The technology stack {#sec-arch-stack}

PhyloTrace is a [Shiny](https://shiny.posit.co) application [@shiny] structured
with [Rhino](https://appsilon.github.io/rhino) [@rhino] and the `box` module
system. The layers, from the browser down to the operating system:

| Layer | Technology | Role |
|---|---|---|
| UI toolkit | `bslib` (Bootstrap 5) | Page layout, navbar, cards, theming, light/dark mode |
| Reactive server | `shiny` | The reactive engine and the client–server bridge |
| App structure | `rhino` + `box` | Module boundaries, namespacing, build of JS/SCSS assets |
| Front-end assets | SCSS + vanilla JS | Styling and small browser-side behaviours (@sec-arch-frontend) |
| Persistence | SQLite via `RSQLite` | The portable per-database `.db` file (@sec-arch-state) |
| R libraries | `renv` lockfile | ~40 R packages (`ape`, `ggtree`, `igraph`, `leaflet`, …) |
| External tools | Conda environment | pyMLST, AMRFinderPlus, `blat`, `mafft`, abritamr (@sec-arch-conda) |

The two dependency worlds — the R packages under `renv` and the command-line
tools under Conda — are kept strictly separate (@sec-arch-conda).

::: {.callout-important title="The app runs under system R, not the Conda env"}
The Shiny app itself runs under **system R with its `renv` library**
(`dependencies.R` + `renv.lock`). The Conda environment named `PhyloTrace` holds
*only* the external CLI toolchain the app shells out to. This is stated verbatim
at the top of `environment.yml`:

```{.yaml filename="environment.yml"}
# The Shiny app itself does NOT run from this env: it runs under system R with
# its renv library (dependencies.R + renv.lock). Keep the two separate — the
# conda env is the tools, renv is the R packages.
```
:::

## How the app boots {#sec-arch-boot}

The entry point is deliberately tiny. `app.R` at the repository root does
nothing but hand control to Rhino:

```{.r filename="app.R"}
# Rhino / shinyApp entrypoint. Do not edit.
rhino::app()
```

`rhino::app()` is a convention rather than a special mechanism: it loads the
`box` module at `app/main.R` and calls its exported `ui()` and `server()`
functions to obtain a standard Shiny app object. Two small config files shape
the run — `config.yml` sets logging and `rhino.yml` declares that SCSS is
compiled with the `node`-based Sass compiler (`sass: node`). The whole boot
chain is therefore short and fixed:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-boot
%%| fig-cap: "Boot chain. Everything below app/main.R is application code."
flowchart TD
  L["Launcher / run_phylotrace.sh"] --> R["app.R → rhino::app()"]
  R --> Cfg["config.yml · rhino.yml"]
  R --> M["app/main.R<br/>(exports ui() and server())"]
  M --> UI["ui(): page_navbar + splash"]
  M --> SRV["server(): wires every module,<br/>owns the shared reactive signals"]
```

`app/main.R` is the root `box` module. Like every Rhino view module it exports
exactly two functions — the `ui(id)`/`server(id)` template every module follows
(@sec-arch-modules). The navbar's version badge is not hard-coded; it reads the
single source of truth in `app/logic/app_meta.R`:

```{.r filename="app/logic/app_meta.R"}
# Identity of the running application: the single place its version is written
# down, so the badge in the navigation bar and the version stamped into every
# typing provenance row can never drift apart.
```

## The module system {#sec-arch-modules}

PhyloTrace's source lives under `app/` in two sibling trees whose names encode a
hard rule about what may go in each:

- **`app/view/`** — Shiny modules: UI and the reactive server logic that wires it
  up. Every file exports a `ui(id)` and a `server(id)`.
- **`app/logic/`** — application code *independent of Shiny*.

The split is what makes the scientific core testable (@sec-testing) without
simulating clicks, and lets one distance-matrix implementation serve the tree,
the MST and an export without being entangled in any one screen.

### Imports with `box`

Modules never use `library()`. Every dependency is declared explicitly with
`box::use`, in two blocks: first R packages, then other app modules. The project
convention (`AGENTS.md`) requires the imports to be alphabetical and to list
only what is actually used. The second block of `app/main.R` *is* the top-level
module map of the application, plus the handful of logic modules the root wires
in directly:

```{.r filename="app/main.R"}
box::use(
  app / logic / app_meta[APP_VERSION],
  app / logic / database_functions[migrate_species_name, sync_metadata_table],
  app / logic / db_events[bump_all, new_bus],
  app / logic / db_store[new_store],
  app / logic / functions[render_info],
  app / logic / logging[log_event, start_session_log],
  app / logic / paths[stat_json, app_local_share_path],
  app / logic / pymlst[hash_database, hashes_pending],
  app / view / landing_page,
  app / view / scheme_browser,
  app / view / database,
  app / view / typing,
  app / view / analysis_dashboard,
  app / view / visualization,
)
```

::: {.callout-important title="Namespacing: how a module gets its own piece of the screen"}
Each module instance is given an `id`. Inside `ui()`, `ns <- NS(id)` turns a
local input name like `"generate"` into a globally-unique one like
`"visualization-plot3-generate"`. Inside `server()`, `session$ns` does the same.
This is what lets several instances of the *same* module — say, three MST plot
tabs — coexist without their inputs colliding. When you read `input$generate` in
a module, it is always that module's own `generate`.
:::

## The module tree {#sec-arch-tree}

`app/main.R` composes six top-level view modules, and three of those are
coordinators that instantiate further modules of their own. Every one of the
nodes below is a Shiny module with its own `ui()`/`server()` pair and its own
namespace — there are no "half modules" in the tree:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-module-tree
%%| fig-cap: "The full module tree. Every node is a Shiny module with its own ui()/server() and namespace. Solid edges are composition; the multiplicity labels mark the three coordinators that instantiate their children dynamically, once per plot tab, Analysis and saved Plot."
flowchart LR
  main["app/main.R<br/><i>root · navbar · signal bus</i>"]

  main --> lp["landing_page<br/><i>load / create a .db</i>"]
  main --> sb["scheme_browser<br/><i>download cgMLST schemes</i>"]
  main --> ty["typing<br/><i>Add Isolates</i>"]
  main --> db["database<br/><i>Database sub-app</i>"]
  main --> ad["analysis_dashboard<br/><i>Tier 3 · saved analyses</i>"]
  main --> vz["visualization<br/><i>plot workspace</i>"]

  db --> dbb["database_browser<br/><i>Browse Entries</i>"]
  db --> dbc["database_custom<br/><i>Custom Variables</i>"]
  db --> dbg["database_cgmlst<br/><i>cgMLST Overview</i>"]
  db --> dbi["database_import<br/><i>Import</i>"]
  db --> dbe["database_export<br/><i>Export</i>"]

  ad -- "1 per Analysis" --> grp["analysis_dashboard/group<br/><i>Tier 2</i>"]
  grp -- "1 per saved Plot" --> itm["analysis_dashboard/item<br/><i>Tier 1</i>"]

  vz -- "1 per plot tab" --> vp["visualization_plot<br/><i>sidebar + one engine</i>"]
  vp --> vmst["visualization_mst"]
  vp --> vtree["visualization_tree"]
  vp --> vepi["visualization_epi"]
  vp --> vmap["visualization_map"]
  vp --> vamr["visualization_amr"]
```

The six top-level modules map to the panels the user sees:

| Module | Panel | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| `landing_page` | Load Database | this chapter (@sec-arch-nav) |
| `scheme_browser` | Scheme Browser | @sec-tech-schemes |
| `typing` | Add Isolates | @sec-tech-typing |
| `database` | Database Browser | @sec-tech-browser |
| `analysis_dashboard` | Analysis Dashboard | @sec-tech-dashboard |
| `visualization` | Visualization | @sec-tech-visualization |

The three coordinators differ in *when* they instantiate their children.
`database` mounts its five panels once, at startup, in a fixed set
(@sec-arch-subapp). `visualization` and `analysis_dashboard` instantiate theirs
dynamically — one `visualization_plot` per open plot tab (which in turn starts
exactly one of the five engine servers, fixed for that tab's lifetime), one
`group` per Analysis, one `item` per saved Plot (@sec-arch-nested).

## Dynamic navigation: from landing page to workspace {#sec-arch-nav}

The app does not show all its panels at once. On startup the navbar carries only
two: **Load Database** and **Scheme Browser**. The four workspace panels are
*inserted at runtime* the moment a database is loaded, and removed again on
reset. This keeps every data-facing module from trying to query a database that
is not open yet.

The trigger is the landing page. It exposes a `db_path` reactive that is `NULL`
until the user actually presses **Load**, which is what gates the whole app:

```{.r filename="app/view/landing_page.R"}
# `db_path` is the *loaded* database, not merely the selected or remembered one.
# ... Gating on `load_trigger()` (NULL until Load is pressed ...) keeps every
# downstream module from querying - or migrating - a file the user has not
# asked for yet.
db_path = shiny$reactive(
  if (is.null(load_trigger())) NULL else db_location()[2]
)
```

When Load fires, `main.R` opens a session log, shows a full-page loading
overlay, runs three deterministic on-load migrations, announces them on the
revision bus, then builds and inserts the four workspace panels:

```{.r filename="app/main.R"}
observeEvent(LANDING_PAGE_vals$load_database(), {
  db_path <- LANDING_PAGE_vals$db_path()

  start_session_log(if (length(db_path)) db_path else NA_character_)

  w <- Waiter$new(..., html = div(spin_flower(), tags$h5("Loading Database ...")))
  w$show()

  # Bring the scheme species up to the current spelling, backfill any missing
  # allele hashes, then create/sync the metadata table — one explicit,
  # deterministic sync every module's read can rely on instead of each doing
  # its own lazily.
  migrate_species_name(db_path)
  hash_database(db_path)
  sync_metadata_table(db_path)
  bump_all(db_rev)          # every reader re-queries (see the signal bus below)

  app_panels <- list(
    fillable_panel("Database Browser",   value = "database_panel",  ...),
    fillable_panel("Analysis Dashboard", value = "analysis_dashboard_panel", ...),
    fillable_panel("Visualization",      value = "visualization_panel", ...),
    fillable_panel("Add Isolates",       value = "typing_panel", ...)
  )
  for (i in seq_along(app_panels)) {
    nav_insert(id = "tabs", nav = app_panels[[i]], target = targets[i],
               position = "after", select = i == 1L)
  }
  nav_hide(id = "tabs", target = "landing_page_panel")
  nav_hide(id = "tabs", target = "scheme_browser_panel")
})
```

Two implementation details are relevant here. The panel UI is wrapped in
`strip_shinyfiles_assets()` before insertion — a `tagQuery` pass that removes
duplicate `shinyFiles` `<script>`/`<link>` tags that would otherwise be injected
once per panel. The three on-load calls also run *before* any module reads the
file, which is why the landing page gates `db_path` behind the Load press — the
details of what those migrations do are in @sec-database.

## The reactive signal bus {#sec-arch-signals}

Modules do not call each other directly. They communicate through a small set of
**shared reactive values** owned by `main.R`, plus the named lists of reactives
each module *returns*. This mechanism coordinates state across the whole app.

Four broadcast signals plus one shared cache flow out of `main.R`:

```{.r filename="app/main.R"}
# Returns the user to the landing screen. Only Landing Page + Scheme Browser
# listen (so a stale remembered db_path isn't re-loaded).
session_reset <- reactiveVal(0L)

# "Tear down and re-query": bumped on a full reset AND on "Reload Database".
data_reset <- reactiveVal(0L)

# Bumped once a freshly built set of app panels is actually in the DOM, so each
# module can re-apply the DOM state it drives from the server.
ui_mounted <- reactiveVal(0L)

# Per-domain revision counters for the loaded database (app/logic/db_events.R):
# writers bump the domains they touch, readers depend on the domains they read.
db_rev <- new_bus()
```

The revision bus is the central design decision behind this signal set; its
source comment is reproduced here in full:

```{.r filename="app/main.R"}
# A SQLite write is invisible to Shiny's reactive graph: db_path() does not
# change, so a reader keyed only on it never re-queries and quietly shows
# data from before the write. Every module that writes bumps the domains it
# touched; every module that reads names the domains it depends on. This
# supersedes the per-pair signals the app grew one at a time (Analyses/plots,
# custom variables, staged sets, typed isolates), which each covered exactly
# one edge of that graph and left the rest stale.
```

`app/logic/db_events.R` defines the domains a write can touch — `isolates`,
`metadata`, `custom_fields`, `amr`, `staged` — deliberately coarse: "one counter
per domain rather than one per table … a domain is the smallest unit any reader
distinguishes." On top of the bus sits one shared cache, `app/logic/db_store.R`,
the single reactive that reads the `metadata` table:

```{.r filename="app/logic/db_store.R"}
# The one reactive that reads the loaded database's `metadata` table, shared
# by every module that displays it (Database Browser, Visualization, Analysis
# Dashboard, Export). ... A store makes that structural instead of
# conventional: there is exactly one reactive that reads the table, so there is
# exactly one place that can get the dependency list wrong ...
```

Each module is started with the signals, the store and the `db_path` it needs,
and returns a list of reactives that `main.R` (and sibling modules) observe:

```{.r filename="app/main.R"}
TYPING_vals <- typing$server("typing",
  db_path = LANDING_PAGE_vals$db_path, session_reset = data_reset, db_rev = db_rev)

DATABASE_vals <- database$server("database",
  db_path = LANDING_PAGE_vals$db_path, session_reset = data_reset,
  show_browse = show_browse, ui_mounted = ui_mounted, db_rev = db_rev, store = store)
```

The full signal flow — who owns each signal and who reacts to it:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-signals
%%| fig-cap: "The reactive signal bus. Solid arrows are shared signals/caches owned by main.R; dashed arrows are values a module returns and its siblings observe."
flowchart LR
  subgraph MAIN["app/main.R"]
    SR(["session_reset"])
    DR(["data_reset"])
    REV(["db_rev (revision bus)"])
    ST(["store (metadata cache)"])
    DBP(["db_path (from landing_page)"])
  end

  SR --> lp["landing_page"]
  SR --> sb["scheme_browser"]
  SR --> vz["visualization"]

  DR --> ty["typing"]
  DR --> db["database"]
  DR --> ad["analysis_dashboard"]

  DBP --> ty & db & ad & vz
  REV --> ty & db & ad & vz
  ST --> db & ad & vz
  ty -. "bumps db_rev(isolates,amr)" .-> REV
  db -. "bumps db_rev(metadata,custom_fields,staged)" .-> REV

  ty -. "db_updated" .-> MAIN
  db -. "pending / imported" .-> MAIN
  ad -. "request_add_plot / request_open_plot" .-> MAIN
  MAIN -. "nav_select + launch_ctx" .-> vz
```

::: {.callout-important title="Two reset signals, and why the bus is separate from both"}
`session_reset` and `data_reset` look redundant but are not. `data_reset` means
"every data module tears down its reactive state and re-queries" — used both on
a full reset *and* on the lightweight **Reload Database**. `session_reset`
additionally sends Landing Page and Scheme Browser back to their pre-load state.
The revision bus `db_rev` is different again: it says *"re-read, your query is
out of date"*, not *"tear down, the session moved"* — so a module holding
unsaved user input (the Database Browser's edit grid) can treat a bump as a
staleness marker rather than a cue to discard the user's work. Visualization is
the one module wired to `session_reset` rather than `data_reset`, because it
tears its plot tabs down only when their nav markup is being removed too.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="There is no global 'current state'"}
No single variable holds "the currently selected isolates" or "the open
database" for every part of the app to read and write. Each module keeps its own
state, and the revision bus keeps them synchronized: *"the isolate pool changed
— everyone who reads it, re-read it."* This is what lets loading a new database,
or reloading after typing, refresh every table and plot without any module
reaching into another. A new module that reads the database must therefore
declare the domains it depends on; one that writes must bump them.
:::

## Composition pattern 1 — the Database sub-app {#sec-arch-subapp}

The **Database Browser** panel is itself a sub-application. `app/view/database.R`
defines a sidebar menu and, for each entry, a hidden tab panel hosting a
sub-module under its own namespace. The menu is data:

```{.r filename="app/view/database.R"}
db_menu <- list(
  list(value = "browse_entries",  label = "Browse Entries",  module = database_browser),
  list(value = "custom_fields",   label = "Custom Variables", module = database_custom),
  list(value = "cgmlst_overview", label = "cgMLST Overview",  module = database_cgmlst),
  list(value = "import",          label = "Import",           module = database_import),
  list(value = "export",          label = "Export",           module = database_export)
)
```

The UI turns that list into a `navset_hidden` with one panel per entry, and the
server starts each sub-module's server in a loop, forwarding `db_path`,
`session_reset` and the revision bus `db_rev`, and passing the shared `store` and
`ui_mounted` only to the sub-modules that need them:

```{.r filename="app/view/database.R"}
for (item in db_menu) {
  extra <- switch(item$value,
    browse_entries = list(store = store),
    import         = list(ui_mounted = ui_mounted),
    export         = list(ui_mounted = ui_mounted, store = store),
    list())
  result <- do.call(item$module$server,
    c(list(item$value, db_path = db_path, session_reset = session_reset,
           db_rev = db_rev), extra))
  ...
}
```

This "menu + hidden tabset + forwarded signals" pattern is the same shape as the
top-level navbar in `main.R`, one level down.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-subapp
%%| fig-cap: "The Database sub-app. One coordinator dispatches to five independent sub-modules via a hidden tabset; each runs its own server under its own namespace."
flowchart TD
  d["app/view/database.R<br/><i>sidebar menu + navset_hidden</i>"]
  d --> b["database_browser<br/><i>Browse Entries</i>"]
  d --> c["database_custom<br/><i>Custom Variables</i>"]
  d --> g["database_cgmlst<br/><i>cgMLST Overview</i>"]
  d --> i["database_import<br/><i>Import</i>"]
  d --> e["database_export<br/><i>Export</i>"]
```

## Composition pattern 2 — nested modules (the Analysis Dashboard) {#sec-arch-nested}

The Analysis Dashboard shows the deepest nesting in the app: three tiers, each
its own module, labelled as such in the source.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-nested
%%| fig-cap: "Three-tier module nesting in the Analysis Dashboard. Tier 2 is instantiated once per Analysis and Tier 1 once per saved Plot, so the tree's width follows the data."
flowchart TD
  t3["analysis_dashboard.R<br/><b>Tier 3</b> — the dashboard"]
  t2["analysis_dashboard/group.R<br/><b>Tier 2</b> — one Analysis"]
  t1["analysis_dashboard/item.R<br/><b>Tier 1</b> — one saved Plot"]
  t3 -- "1 per Analysis" --> t2
  t2 -- "1 per saved Plot" --> t1
```

- **Tier 1** (`item.R`) — *"a single saved Plot, rendered as a value box with a
  live thumbnail."*
- **Tier 2** (`group.R`) — *"one Analysis container. Holds the saved Plot boxes
  for a single [analysis]."*
- **Tier 3** (`analysis_dashboard.R`) — *"lists the Analyses stored in the
  loaded database and lets the user add/navigate them."*

The dashboard bubbles two requests up to `main.R` — `request_add_plot` and
`request_open_plot` — which `main.R` turns into a `nav_select()` to the
Visualization tab plus a launch/restore context (the dashed hand-off in
@fig-signals). The persistence behind all three tiers lives in
`app/logic/analysis_store.R`, inside the loaded `.db` itself
(@sec-tech-dashboard).

The Visualization tab uses the same dynamic-instantiation pattern one tier
shallower: the coordinator creates one `visualization_plot` server per open tab,
and that instance starts exactly one of the five engine servers
(@sec-tech-visualization).

## The front-end layer {#sec-arch-frontend}

Not everything is R. A thin browser-side layer handles styling and a few
behaviours that belong in the client:

- **Styling** — `app/styles/main.scss` is compiled (per `rhino.yml`'s `sass:
  node`) to `app/static/css/app.min.css`.
- **JavaScript** — `app/js/index.js` bundles small modules (`busy-shield`,
  `dt-column-sizing`). The most consequential is an input sanitiser that keeps
  anything used to *name* a persisted identifier (a database, scheme or isolate)
  restricted to a filesystem- and SQL-safe character set:

```{.js filename="app/js/index.js"}
// Restrict free-text entry to a filesystem-/SQL-safe character set
// ([a-zA-Z0-9_-]) so anything the user types to *name* an identifier (a
// database, a scheme, an isolate) stays safe to persist, export as a filename,
// and query with.
```

  …while deliberately exempting fields where symbols are legitimate — colour
  pickers, dropdown search boxes, and any display label inside an
  `.allow-free-text` wrapper (plot titles, analysis names).
- **Static assets** — `app/static/` holds images, per-species artwork, and the
  compiled CSS/JS that Rhino serves.

## The boundary to the bioinformatics toolchain {#sec-arch-conda}

Every computationally intensive step that is *not* implemented in R — aligning
an assembly to a scheme, calling AMR genes — happens in external command-line
tools. The app reaches them by shelling out to a single named Conda environment.
The environment name is one source of truth, defined once in
`app/logic/pymlst.R`:

```{.r filename="app/logic/pymlst.R"}
### Single conda environment for every external CLI the app shells out to
# All bioinformatics tooling - cgMLST/classical typing (wgMLST/claMLST + blat +
# mafft) and AMR screening (abritamr/AMRFinderPlus) - lives in one env alongside
# ... Keeping it a single named constant ... is the one source of truth: change
# the env here and every caller follows.
```

The environment's contents are pinned in `environment.yml`:

```{.yaml filename="environment.yml"}
dependencies:
  - python=3.12
  - blat=35            # cgMLST / classical MLST typing (pyMLST toolchain)
  - mafft=7.525
  - abritamr=1.0.19    # AMR screening (blast + hmmer come in transitively)
  - ncbi-amrfinderplus=3.12.8
  - pip
  - pip:
      - pymlst==2.2.2  # pinned, non-editable
```

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-conda
%%| fig-cap: "The process boundary. R (renv) drives external tools in the PhyloTrace Conda env via `conda run`."
flowchart LR
  subgraph RENV["System R + renv (the app)"]
    v1["view/typing.R"] --> l1["logic/pymlst.R"]
    v2["typing"] --> l2["logic/amr.R"]
  end
  subgraph CONDA["Conda env 'PhyloTrace' (external CLIs)"]
    p["pyMLST + blat + mafft"]
    a["abritamr + AMRFinderPlus"]
  end
  l1 -- "conda run -n PhyloTrace" --> p
  l2 -- "conda run -n PhyloTrace" --> a
  p --> DB[("loaded .db")]
  a --> DB
```

The typing details (including `loop-pymlst.sh`, the shell script the wrapper
drives) are in @sec-tech-typing; AMR screening is @sec-tech-amr.

## Where state lives {#sec-arch-state}

PhyloTrace keeps state in exactly three places; distinguishing between them
explains most of its behaviour:

1. **In-session reactive state** — everything transient: selections, generated
   plots, process handles. It lives in each module's `server()` and is wiped by
   `data_reset`/`session_reset` (@sec-arch-signals).
2. **The loaded `.db` file** — the durable, portable core. Every connection to it
   is opened through one helper, `app/logic/db_connect.R`, which arms a busy
   timeout so a query issued while the typing process holds the write lock waits
   rather than fails:

```{.r filename="app/logic/db_connect.R"}
#' How long a statement waits for another writer's lock, in milliseconds.
#' Typing runs pyMLST in a separate process that writes this same file ...
BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS <- 5000L
```

   The file holds the typing data (`mlst`, `sequences`, `hashes`, `metadata`,
   `classical_mlst`), provenance, the AMR tables, the app's own `phylotrace_*`
   tables and the `imported_*` staging tables. Because the app's own data rides
   *inside* the database file, analyses and custom fields travel with it when it
   is shared. Full schema in @sec-database and @sec-appendix-schema.
3. **Local app state** — a tiny `state.json` under the app's local-share
   directory (`app/logic/paths.R`), remembering the last database so the landing
   page can offer "Last used: …". `main.R` writes it on load.

## Chapter summary

- PhyloTrace is a local Shiny web app, structured with Rhino and `box` modules,
  driving external bioinformatics tools through one Conda environment.
- It boots `app.R → rhino::app() → app/main.R`; `main.R` is the root module that
  owns the navbar and the shared reactive signals (@sec-arch-boot,
  @sec-arch-signals).
- Code is split into `app/view` (Shiny modules) and `app/logic` (Shiny-free,
  testable application code) (@sec-arch-modules).
- Every panel and sub-panel is its own Shiny module with its own namespace
  (@fig-module-tree); modules communicate through a per-domain **revision bus**
  and returned reactive lists, never by calling one another directly
  (@fig-signals).
- Two composition patterns recur: the fixed sub-app (Database, @sec-arch-subapp)
  and dynamically instantiated nested modules (Analysis Dashboard and the plot
  tabs, @sec-arch-nested).
- Durable state lives in the portable `.db`; the file *is* the project
  (@sec-arch-state).

**Where to go next:** @sec-database opens up the `.db` schema this chapter kept
referring to; Part II covers the implementation of each component in turn.
